title: He missed the rest
hook: if told someone speaks ill of you, say: he didn't know my other faults (Enchiridion 33)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ask: your own stories please you more than your listeners. Your line was hands the stage to someone else.
screen: `ASK — HANDS THE STAGE TO SOMEONE ELSE.`

segments.voice: A screenshot arrives with a short note above it: thought you should know. Someone has been saying things about you. It's easy to start drafting the reply right there in your head, point by point, with receipts and a closing line. Section thirty-three of the handbook has a one-line answer for this moment, far older than any screenshot. It's short, a little ridiculous, and a very good comeback.
screen: `THOUGHT YOU SHOULD KNOW.` → `ALREADY DRAFTING THE REPLY.` → `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: If someone tells you that a certain person is speaking badly of you, Epictetus says, don't defend yourself against what was said. Instead, answer: he obviously didn't know my other faults, or he wouldn't have mentioned only these. Why it works: a defense keeps the argument alive. You go point by point, they answer, the circle grows. His reply steps out of the contest entirely. It agrees, cheerfully, that you have faults, more than the critic knows, so there's nothing left to fight about. The joke is on yourself, and nobody else gets hurt by it. The verb he uses for defend yourself belongs with apologia, a speech of defense, the word in the title of Plato's Apology, where Socrates defends himself at his trial. Epictetus' advice, roughly: skip the apologia. What it isn't: self-hatred, or ignoring a fair point. If the critic is right about something, you've learned something. If they're wrong, nothing that belongs to you has been touched. That idea came up a couple of weeks ago, with the insult: it's not the words that harm you, but your judgment that you've been harmed. Today's line is that idea with a grin on its face. It costs nothing, and it ends the conversation better than any receipt.
screen: `DON'T DEFEND YOURSELF.` · `HE DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.` · `SKIP THE APOLOGIA.` · `A FAIR POINT TEACHES; A WRONG ONE CAN'T HARM.` · then, large: `HE MISSED THE REST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one criticism that still stings, and notice where it lands in your body, and the urge to argue with it. Then try Epictetus' answer inside, he missed the rest, and see if the sting changes; you might even smile. If part of it was fair, let that part stay, and let the rest go.
Apologia. The Greek word for a speech of defense, which Epictetus says to skip: they didn't know my other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. Today's word.
Your line: better than any receipt. A fair point teaches; a wrong one can't touch what's yours. Day three hundred sixty-eight, done.

howItsDone: People practicing Stoicism sometimes answer reported criticism with self-deprecating humor, as Epictetus suggests, rather than defending themselves point by point.
